content.overview: Section 139 requires the first auditor to be appointed by the board within thirty days of registration, and thereafter an auditor to be appointed at the first annual general meeting to hold office until the conclusion of the sixth annual general meeting. Prescribed classes rotate the auditor. A listed company and the other prescribed classes do not appoint an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, or an audit firm for more than two terms.
content.glance: Section 139 requires appointment of an auditor at the first annual general meeting, to hold office until the conclusion of the sixth annual general meeting, with rotation for prescribed classes.
content.study:
## Statutory rule
Section 139(1) requires every company, at the first annual general meeting, to appoint an individual or a firm as auditor, who holds office from the conclusion of that meeting until the conclusion of its sixth annual general meeting, and thereafter until the conclusion of every sixth meeting.

Section 139(2) requires a listed company and the other prescribed classes not to appoint an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, and an audit firm for more than two terms of five consecutive years.

Section 139(6) requires the board to appoint the first auditor within thirty days of registration. If the board does not, the members appoint the first auditor within ninety days.

## Answer structure
Separate the first auditor from the annual-general-meeting appointment. Rotation applies to the classes in subsection (2). Not a verified closure.

sections.heading: Rule
sections.body: The first auditor is appointed by the board within thirty days of incorporation, failing which by the members. Thereafter the appointment is at the AGM for a term ending at the sixth AGM, subject to ratification as the current text requires; amendment history on annual ratification must be checked. Prescribed classes, including listed companies and stated unlisted thresholds, must rotate the individual after one term of five years and the audit firm after two terms, with a five-year cooling off. The auditor must consent and the company must intimate the Registrar. Casual vacancy is filled by the board, or by a general meeting where the vacancy is caused by resignation. Government companies follow CAG appointment under the section.

examples.title: Resignation vacancy
examples.body: A casual vacancy by resignation is filled by the general meeting, not only the board.

examples.title: Rotation
examples.body: A listed-company audit firm cannot simply continue past two consecutive terms.
